explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). In this question, "want" means lacking what he needs, not just wishing for extra things. David is saying the LORD cares for him so fully that he is not left empty.

David does not say he will earn what he needs. He says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). The line is about the LORD's care, not David working his way into being provided for. That shepherd image is all provision, friend.

That is not the word David is aiming at here. He says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). The point is that because the LORD is his shepherd, David will not lack what he needs. Different picture entirely.

That's it. Green pastures and quiet waters paint a calm, cared-for scene in Psalm 23:2. David shows the LORD giving rest, safety, and peace. This is not a frantic sheep sprinting through life with its little wool on fire.

Psalm 23:2 gives the opposite feel from hustle. David says the LORD makes him lie down in green pastures and leads him beside quiet waters. Lying down and quiet waters sound like rest, not grind. This sheep is not checking twelve messages and missing lunch.

Not in this verse. Psalm 23:2 gives green pastures and quiet waters, which sound peaceful and safe. The darker valley comes later in Psalm 23:4, but right here David is painting rest. The mood is calm, not alarm bells.
You got it, baker. David says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). The LORD's care is not only outward, like grass and water. He brings renewal to David's inner life too.
Psalm 23:3 does not say the LORD tests David's soul here. It says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). The line is about renewal and care. David is describing help, not an exam.
That is not the wording in the psalm. David says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). The focus is on the LORD bringing life and refreshment to him. This is a healing line, friend.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: Yes. David says the LORD "guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). The reason David gives is tied to the LORD's own name. His guidance shows who He is.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: That sounds shepherd-ish, but it is not the reason David gives. Psalm 23:3 says the LORD guides him in right paths "for the sake of His name." David points to the LORD's name, not to the flock, as the stated reason. The verse keeps the spotlight on Him.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: Psalm 23:3 does not mention the land here. David says the LORD guides him in paths of righteousness "for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). So the reason in the text is the LORD's name. David is talking about who God is and how He leads.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: Exactly. David says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). The comfort is the LORD's presence in the valley, not the valley disappearing. That is strong, quiet trust.

David does not point to himself. He says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). His confidence rests in the LORD being there with him. Alone is the one thing this verse does not say.

The verse gives no length for the valley. David says, "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). The reason is the LORD's presence. If the Shepherd is there, the fear does not get the last word.
True indeed. David says to the LORD, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). In the valley, those shepherd tools are not a threat to David. They are part of why he has comfort.

The verse actually says the opposite. David says, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). So in that dark valley, the LORD's rod and staff are a comfort to him. Same valley, same shadows, but real comfort.

Yes, friend. David says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). The picture shifts from shepherd and sheep to host and guest. The LORD welcomes David and provides for him.

Psalm 23:5 does not say the LORD prepares a tent. David says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). The image is a host setting a table. It is generous and steady.

That is not the image in this verse. Psalm 23:5 says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." David is describing welcome and provision from the LORD as a host. This is dinner-table care, not bedtime.

The verse does not say the table is far away from David's enemies. It says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). So the enemies are still in view. The point is the LORD's care right there, not somewhere else.

Correct. David says the LORD prepares the table "in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). Not far away from them. The picture is bold, friend. The LORD provides for David even with enemies nearby.
That's the picture. David says, "my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5). Overflow speaks of abundance, not bare survival. The LORD is not measuring out care with an eyedropper here.

David is not describing a spill from clumsiness. He says, "my cup overflows" after speaking of the LORD's generous welcome and care (Psalm 23:5). The image points to plenty. This is abundance, not an oops.
Nothing in Psalm 23:5 suggests hurry. David says, "my cup overflows," which pictures fullness and generosity. The whole verse sounds rich and welcoming. Rushed does not fit this table at all.

Yes. David says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). That is what he expects ahead because of the LORD's care. Not just one lucky season either. All the days.

Those are not the words David uses here. Psalm 23:6 says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." David's hope is centered on the LORD's faithful care. He is talking about goodness and mercy, not status.

Psalm 23:6 names something else. David says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." Those are the two words he chooses as he looks ahead. It is a beautiful pair, and it sticks the landing.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's right. David closes by saying, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). After all the pictures of shepherding and hosting, he ends with lasting nearness to the LORD. That is the final note of the song.
David does not name Hebron here. He says, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). The closing hope is not tied to that city in this verse. It is tied to the LORD's house.
Psalm 23:6 does not end with Canaan. David says, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever." So the place he names is the house of the LORD. That ending lifts the whole psalm upward, friend.
